text: This lab puts the whole chapter together: one real business rule, enforced in two places on the same table, with two different client scripts doing the enforcing. Incident Priority has five real values — Critical, High, Moderate, Low, and Planning — and the rule is that only users holding the incident_manager role may set it to Critical.

On the list, inline-editing the Priority cell never opens a form, so it fires onCellEdit instead. The script checks whether the proposed value is Critical, checks the editing user's role with g_user.hasRole, and if the check fails, sends an error through g_list and calls callback of false, which blocks the pending edit and reverts the cell to its old value. Otherwise it calls callback of true and lets the edit through normally.

The same rule has to hold on the Incident form, or a user could simply open the record and change Priority there instead, bypassing the list entirely. That's a separate onChange script, isolated per Lesson 9's standing rule, running the same role check. But there's no callback here — instead, the script shows the error through g_form and explicitly sets the field back to oldValue to revert it, since onChange has no equivalent to onCellEdit's asynchronous callback.

Four things to hold onto: the list context uses onCellEdit, g_list for messages, and callback of false to block and revert. The form context uses onChange, g_form for messages, and an explicit setValue back to the old value. g_user.hasRole works identically in both, because it's globally available regardless of context. And there's no shortcut — a client script scoped to the list never runs on the form, or the reverse, since they're separate records.

Strip away the mechanics and the actual decision is identical in both scripts: is the new value Critical, and does this user lack the incident_manager role. Only the API for blocking the change — callback versus a manual setValue — differs by context, which is exactly the kind of distinction a CAD-track developer is expected to reason through.
That closes Client Scripts. Chapter 3 opens with Script Includes — the reusable server-side logic that every GlideAjax call from this chapter has actually been calling into all along.
